To THE HONORABLE JOHN G. ROBERTS, JR., CHIEF JUSTICE OF THE UNITED STATES AND
CIRCUIT JUSTICE FOR THE DISTRICT OF COLUMBIA CIRCUIT:
This presents a classic and clear case for a stay of the mandate. The courts
below have ordered a national security reporter, Applicant Catherine V. Herridge, to
hand over her confidential source(s)—presumptively the names of U.S. government
personnel with knowledge of a counterespionage investigation—to a former colonel
in the People's Liberation Army (PLA), the army of the Chinese Communist Party,
who has filed a civil suit against the government under the Privacy Act. See App. Ia
28a (Disclosure Order); Compliance with that order would cause
irreparable harm twice over by depriving Ms. Herridge of her First Amendment
rights and forever disclosing the identity of her confidential source(s). Both lower
courts adjudicated this important case without inflicting that irreparable harm—the
district court that ordered disclosure stayed its own contempt order to allow orderly
appellate review, and the Court of Appeals took over two years to deliberate with that
stay in place. This Court should give itself the same opportunity for orderly review
by staying the issuance of the mandate.
Accordingly, pursuant to Rule 23 of the Rules of this Court and the All Writs
Act, 28 U.S.C. 51651, Ms. Herridge respectfully seeks an order staying issuance of
the mandate from the court of appeals pending the filing and disposition of a petition
for a writ of certiorari. Given the exigent circumstances, she requests that the
Court act by noon on Monday, June 29, 2026 to stay the issuance of the
mandate pending disposition of this application or to issue an
administrative stay to preserve the status quo while the Court considers
1

this application.
This case underscores the importance of reporting based on confidential
sources. In 2017, Ms. Herridge was the lead reporter on a series of stories about
counterespionage concerns with Plaintiff, a former colonel in the PLA who was
running a university catering to U.S. military personnel and gathering information
on thousands of U.S. servicemembers in the process. Making matters worse, the
Department of Defense (DOD) itself was effectively funding this whole enterprise
through a tuition assistance program. In 2018, following Herridge's reporting, DOD
conducted an independent inquiry and publicly terminated the university from the
tuition assistance program "on national security grounds." Rather than challenge
that termination decision as arbitrary, capricious, or otherwise erroneous, Plaintiff
sued the government under the Privacy Act, claiming that information from
government files that had appeared in Ms. Herridge's stories caused DOD to reach
its decision. In that civil lawsuit, Plaintiff subpoenaed Herridge, and the courts below
have rejected Ms. Herridge's claim of reporter's privilege and ordered her to turn over
the name(s) of her confidential national security source(s) to a former PLA colonel
whom DOD found to be a national security risk. That order has been stayed while
the lower courts adjudicated the important issues raised by Ms. Herridge's claim of
reporter's privilege, and a stay of the mandate will preserve the status quo to permit
this Court's orderly review of those issues.
This case raises vitally important questions about both: (i) the standards for
applying the First Amendment reporter's privilege, and (ii) whether this Court should
2

recognize a reporter's privilege under federal common law. All the factors this Court
considers overwhelmingly favor maintaining the status quo pending Ms. Herridge's
forthcoming petition for certiorari.
First, there is at least a reasonable probability that the Court will grant
certiorari because the decision below conflicts with decisions of other circuits. The
D.C. Circuit held that the First Amendment reporter's privilege turns on a stark two-
factor test that considers only: (1) whether the information sought (here, the identity
of sources) is "central" to the plaintiffs case, and (2) whether the plaintiff exhausted
alternative avenues of discovery. Because the identity of a source is always central
in a Privacy Act case (among other things, to prove willfulness and intent), that test
reduces the privilege to a mere exhaustion requirement under which a plaintiff
always gets access to confidential sources eventually. That approach conflicts with
the test applied by other circuits, which engage in a genuine balancing to weigh the
plaintiffs interest in disclosure against society's interest in the "free flow of
information" to the press—a balancing that allows courts to, among things,
distinguish between civil and criminal cases. Bruno & Stillman, Inc. v. Globe
Newspaper Co., 633 F.2d 583, 596 (1st Cir. 1980). Those circuits recognize that
protecting society's interest in the functioning of the press may outweigh a plaintiffs
needs in a particular case. This case would almost certainly have come out differently
in those circuits: Ms. Herridge introduced evidence that her effectiveness as a
national security reporter would be destroyed if she were forced to divulge her
source(s) to a former PLA colonel. And that interest unquestionably outweighs
3

Plaintiffs interest in a civil suit that may ultimately amount to nothing more than
$1,000 in statutory damages, even if successful.
The decision below also deepens an acknowledged circuit split on whether to
recognize a reporter's privilege under Rule 501 of the Federal Rules of Evidence,
through which Congress expressly authorized federal courts to define new privileges
by interpreting "[t]he common law ... in the light of reason and experience." The D.C.
Circuit joined several other circuits in declining to recognize a non-constitutional
privilege, notwithstanding its miserly view of the First Amendment privilege. That
decision squarely conflicts with the Third Circuit's decision in Riley v. City of Chester,
612 F.2d 708, 715 (3d Cir. 1979), which not only recognizes a non-constitutional
privilege under common law principles, but also requires courts to "balance on one
hand the policies which give rise to the privilege and their applicability to the facts
at hand against the need for the evidence sought to be obtained," id. at 716—which
is precisely what the D.C. Circuit refused to do.
Second, there is at least a fair prospect that the Court would reverse. Whether
under the First Amendment or federal common law, there is a fair prospect that the
Court will hold that a former PLA colonel's need to obtain the identity of Ms.
Herridge's confidential source(s)—presumptively U.S. government official(s)—in this
civil case does not outweigh Ms. Herridge's interest in maintaining the confidentiality
of her source(s) and the public's interest in national security reporting. As a matter
of First Amendment law, the D.C. Circuit's mechanical two-factor test amounts to a
rule of automatic disclosure of confidential sources in virtually every case where a
4

plaintiff needs the information no matter how low the stakes for the plaintiff or how
high the costs to the fourth estate, chilling the free flow of information to the press
and undermining its ability to fulfill the "essential role in our democracy ' of 'bar[ing]
the secrets of government and inform[ing] the people." N.Y. 'Iimes Co. v. United
States, 403 U.S. 713, 717 (1971) (Black, J., concurring). This case perfectly illustrates
the importance of confidential sources and the centrality of a reporter's privilege to
the First Amendment's distinct textual protection of the freedom of the press. Ms.
Herridge's interest in keeping secret the identity of her source(s)—(presumptively)
government personnel with information critical to rooting out improper foreign
influences—could not be more compelling, while Plaintiffs need for the information
in this low-stakes civil matter is relatively trivial. Only by applying a test that
systematically underweights First Amendment values could the D.C. Circuit
conclude that disclosure was warranted.
As a matter of federal common law, the D.C. Circuit's approach is even worse.
In enacting Rule 501 of the Federal Rules of Evidence, Congress expressly authorized
federal courts to define new privileges by interpreting "[t]he common law ... in the
light of reason and experience." Where the Court has applied Rule 501 to recognize
a psychotherapist-patient privilege, see Jaffee v. Redmond, 518 U.S. 1 (1996), there
is (at the very least) a "fair prospect" that the Court would recognize a privilege
shielding reporters from the forced disclosure of confidential sources. See 23 Charles
A. Wright & Kenneth W. Graham, Federal Practice & Procedure 55426 (1980 & Supp.
2013) ("Congress expected that Rule 501 would be used to create a privilege for
5

newsmen."). At least 48 states and the District of Columbia have recognized a
reporter's privilege. It would defy "reason and experience" to refuse to recognize the
same privilege in federal court either as a matter of constitutional law or common
law principles. Fed. R. Evid. 501.
Third, absent a stay, Ms. Herridge will suffer irreparable harm twice over.
"The loss of First Amendment freedoms, for even minimal periods of time,
unquestionably constitutes irreparable injury." Roman Catholic Diocese of Brooklyn
v. Cuomo, 592 U.S. 14, 19 (2020) (quoting Elrod v. Burns, 427 U.S. 347, 373 (1976)
(plurality)). If the order requiring disclosure is put into effect, Ms. Herridge's pledge
of confidentiality would irremediably be breached, and the identity of the source(s)
would forever be disclosed. No court would be able to undo that disclosure, which is
why the courts below kept a stay in place while they adjudicated.
Fourth, maintaining the status quo will not materially harm Plaintiff. At
worst, a stay would merely postpone disclosure—if the order below is ultimately
affirmed. The district court itself recognized there was no urgency to disclosing Ms.
Herridge's source(s) as it stayed its own contempt order pending appeal, and the court
of appeals kept that stay in place while it deliberated over two years. Extending that
stay by a few months to allow this Court time to consider a petition for certiorari will
not cause any material harm.
Fifth, the public interest favors a stay. As amici as diverse as Senator Ted
Cruz and the New York Times underscored below, the public has a critical interest in
First Amendment protections promoting the flow of information to the press,
6

especially in matters involving national security. If the decision below stands,
sources everywhere will now think twice about sharing important and confidential
information with reporters for fear that their identity will be exposed in civil
litigation. The decision below should be recognized for what it is: A profound threat
to the First Amendment and the press's ability to "bare the secrets of government
and inform the people." N.Y. Times Co., 403 U.S. at 717 (Black, J., concurring).
DECISIONS BELOW
The Contempt Order requiring Ms. Herridge to disclose her confidential
source(s) and setting a fine of $800 a day is reproduced at App. 29a—52a. The D.C.
Circuit's order affirming the district court is reproduced at App. 53a—64a. The D.C.
Circuit's order denying a motion to stay the mandate is reproduced at App. 67a.
JURISDICTION
This Court has jurisdiction over an application for a stay pending review under
28 U.S.C. #1254 and 1651. The district court stayed its Contempt Order through a
timely appeal. App. 52a. The D.C. Circuit denied a motion to stay issuance of its
mandate. App. 67a. Once the mandate issues, the district court's stay will expire.
Thus, the relief sought here is not available in any other court. Sup. Ct. R. 23(3).
A.
BACKGROUND AND PROCEDURAL HISTORY
The Counterespionage Investigation into Plaintiff and
Ms. Herridge's Reporting
Ms. Herridge was the lead reporter on three Fox News stories in 2017 (the "Fox
Reportin*) describing a counterespionage investigation into Plaintiff Yanping Chen,
the founder of the University of Management and Technology (UMT). The stories
7

reported evidence that Plaintiff had been a colonel in the People's Liberation Army
and that she sought to hide that fact by lying on immigration forms to become a U.S.
citizen and telling others to lie under oath to conceal her past. App. 73a—81a.
Nearly all of the Fox Reporting was based on information obtained from non-
government and non-confidential sources. Among other things, the stories featured
on-camera interviews with Stephen Rhoads, a whistleblower and former UMT
employee who had served as an FBI informant. ld. Rhoads explained that Plaintiff
had admitted to him that she had been a PLA colonel and instructed him to lie about
that fact when he testified before a federal grand jury: "Oh, you don't tell them
anything .... You don't—you don't know I was a colonel in the P.L.A. They'll never
have proof to say that." ld. at 74a—75a. Rhoads also explained that UMT was
collecting information about U.S. servicemembers' military history that could then be
remotely accessed. ld. at 75a. An expert on the Chinese military, Peter Mattis,
explained that the personnel records would provide a "curated database" that would
be of interest to the PLA for two reasons: "The first is, militaries everywhere want to
know what a potential adversary might look like—what are their capabilities, how
will they act? The second is this might also serve as a vehicle for recruiting
individuals." ld. at 78a.1
Rhoads explained that UMT was receiving $250,000 to $300,000 per month in
taxpayer dollars from DOD through a tuition assistance program. ld. at 77a. As

The stories explained that the FBI and the U.S. Attorney's Office disagreed
about taking action against Plaintiff based in part on concerns about disclosing
intelligence sources and methods.2 ld. at 75a. In addition, the Naval Criminal
Investigative Service (NCIS) confirmed on the record that there was "still an active

Finally, the stories included some information that Plaintiff later claimed had

however, almost all of the information Plaintiff identified as the basis for her Privacy
Act claims—with the exception of photographs of her in her PLA colonel's uniform—
was already a matter of public record in the Eastern District of Virginia in the

terminating UMT from the tuition assistance program "on national security
grounds."4 DOD determined that

C. Plaintiff Sues the Government Under the Privacy Act and
Subpoenas Ms. Herridge To Uncover Her Confidential Source(s)
Plaintiff never challenged any of DOD's findings in court. Instead, she sued
several agencies under the Privacy Act seeking to have the federal government
compensate her for her lost revenue when DOD found that she was a national security
threat and cut off taxpayer funding for UMT. Although she did not sue Ms. Herridge,
she sought to blame her losses on an alleged leak of Privacy Act information to Ms.
Herridge. Plaintiffs theory was that, if Ms. Herridge had not run her stories, DOD
never would have stumbled onto what Plaintiff was up to (or never would have done
anything about it), so Ms. Herridge's reporting supposedly "caused" DOD to reach its
independent decision to cut off Plaintiffs funds "on national security grounds."
In June 2022, Plaintiff served subpoenas seeking to uncover Ms. Herridge's
confidential source(s). Ms. Herridge moved to quash, asserting a reporter's privilege
under both the First Amendment and FRE 501. Ms. Herridge argued that, under
established precedent, the district court needed to weigh the public interest in
protecting the reporter's sources against the private interest in compelling disclosure.
That weighing tipped decisively in favor of non-disclosure for multiple reasons,
including: (1) the fact that nearly all of the Fox Reporting involved public information,
limiting Plaintiffs potential damages and the magnitude of her claim; (2) the fact
11

that DOD made an independent decision to terminate UMT's contract on national
security grounds, thereby breaking any chain of causation between any Privacy Act
violation and Plaintiffs alleged damages; (3) the risk that Plaintiff is using her
Privacy Act suit to have the government pay her compensation for passing
information to the CCP; (4) the immense harm that forced disclosure would do to Ms.
Herridge's ability to work as a national security reporter; and (5) the importance of
confidential sources to national security reporting and the public's interest in
protecting the ability of the press to provide such reporting—especially where, as
here, the reporting exposed what DOD confirmed was a real national security risk.
The district court denied in relevant part the motion to quash and ordered Ms.
Herridge to disclose her confidential source(s). Disclosure Order, App. la—28a. The
court held that two factors controlled analysis of the First Amendment reporteFs
privilege: (I) whether the information sought is central to the plaintiffs case
("centrality") and (2) whether the plaintiff exhausted reasonable alternative avenues
of discovery ("exhaustion"). See id. at IOa—IIa. As Ms. Herridge pointed out, because
the identity of a source is always deemed "central" to a Privacy Act claim (because
the plaintiff needs the source to prove willfulness and intent), a test focused on solely
"centrality ' and "exhaustion" is really nothing more than an exhaustion requirement
under which every plaintiff always gets access to a reporter's confidential sources
eventually.
The district court also declined to recognize a reporter's privilege under
Federal Rule of Evidence 501. ld. at 25a—27a.
12

D. The District Court Holds Ms. Herridge in Contempt and the
Court of Appeals Affirms
When Ms. Herridge subsequently declined to identify her source(s) at
deposition, the district court held Ms. Herridge in contempt. Contempt Order, App.
52a. The court set a civil contempt fine of $800 per day, but stayed its order "until
completion of proceedings on a timely appeal." ld.
On appeal, the D.C. Circuit affirmed, holding that the analysis for applying the
First Amendment reporter's privilege is limited to the two factors of centrality and
exhaustion after taking some two years to deliberate while the stay remained in
place.5 ld. at 62a—63a. The court also refused to recognize a reporter's privilege
under the auspices of Federal Rule of Evidence 501. ld. at 63a—64a. The court of
appeals subsequently denied rehearing and rehearing en banc after taking five and
a half months to consider the request, Orders, Chen v. FBI, No. 24-5050 (D.C. Cir.
May 22, 2026), Nos. 2174726, 2174732.
Ms. Herridge moved to stay issuance of the mandate, and the court granted a
joint motion for a briefing schedule making her reply brief due on June 23, 2026. App.
66a. On June 23, however, before Ms. Herridge even had a chance to file her reply
brief, the court denied the motion to stay the mandate. ld. 67a.
REASONS FOR GRANTING THE APPLICATION
This case presents the classic circumstances in which a stay of the mandate is
necessary to allow the orderly functioning of the appellate process. Absent a stay,
5 The D.C. Circuit acknowledged that a court could also assure itself that the plaintiffs case was not
'frivolous" before ordering disclosure. ld. at 60a.
13

Ms. Herridge will be subject to an order overriding First Amendment protections and
forcing her to disclose her confidential source(s). There will be no way to reverse that
disclosure or eliminate that irremediable First Amendment injury. That is why the
lower courts maintained a stay over their years of deliberations. A much shorter
extension of the stay is warranted to preserve the status quo during this Court's
deliberations and to prevent both the irreparable harm to Ms. Herridge's First
Amendment rights and the irreversible disclosure of her source(s).
In contrast to the severe and irreversible harms to Ms. Herridge, there is no
urgency that warrants precipitously forcing Ms. Herridge to disclose her source(s)
before this Court has an opportunity to consider a petition for certiorari. The
underlying dispute is a civil case seeking damages—not a criminal prosecution or
civil case seeking emergency relief. The district court proceeded accordingly. It has
overseen this litigation for seven and a half years, stayed its own contempt order
almost two and half years ago, and recognized that there was no need for the case to
move forward during appellate review. The district court rightly held that Ms.
Herridge should be allowed to "litigate her First Amendment claim to the hilt before
revealing her source" because "it is better to be safe than sorry when it comes to First
Amendment rights." Contempt Order, App. 51a. The D.C. Circuit had the benefit of
that stay for more than two years while it considered the case. Granting a stay of the
D.C. Circuit's mandate would put this Court in the same position as the D.C.
Circuit—having the ability to address the case on the Court's usual schedule, without
the urgent press of a possible First Amendment injury. The balance of equities tips
14

strongly in favor of extending the stay and avoiding an irrevocable step that this
Court later may decide violates Ms. Herridge's First Amendment rights.
A stay is warranted when there is "(I) a reasonable probability that four
Justices will consider the issue sufficiently meritorious to grant certiorari; (2) a fair
prospect that a majority of the Court will vote to reverse the judgment below; and
(3) a likelihood that irreparable harm will result from the denial of a stay."
Hollingsworth v. Perry, 558 U.S. 183, 190 (2010) (per curiam); accord Maryland v.
King, 567 U.S. 1301, 1302 (2012) (Roberts, C.J., in chambers). Additionally, in "a
close case it may be appropriate to 'balance the equities'—to explore the relative
harms to applicant and respondent, as well as the interests of the public at large."
Rostker v. Goldberg, 448 U.S. 1306, 1308 (1980) (Brennan, J. , in chambers). All these
factors weigh decisively in favor of a stay.
1.
There Is a Reasonable Probability This Court Will Grant Certiorari.
A. The Decision Below on the First Amendment Reporter's
Privilege Creates a Conflict with Several Other Circuits and
State Courts of Last Resort and Warrants Review by This Court.
The decision below endorsing a mechanical, two-factor test for applying the
First Amendment reporter's privilege conflicts with decisions of at least the First,
Fourth, Ninth, and Tenth Circuits. Those courts, as well as several state supreme
courts, engage in a broader analysis that weighs the plaintiffs interest in disclosure
of a source against society's interest in the "free flow of information" to the press.
Bruno, 633 F.2d at 596. The square conflict in the standards used to determine the
application of a crucial constitutional privilege warrants review by this Court.
15

Under the D.C. Circuit's decision, the reporter's privilege always fails if the
information sought from a reporter is (1) central to the case and (2) the movant has
exhausted other sources for getting the information. See App. 62a—63a. Worse still,
because circuit precedent always treats the identity of a source as "central" to a
Privacy Act claim (in order to prove intent and willfulness, see Lee v. Dep't of Justice,
413 F.3d 53, 60 (D.C. Cir. 2005)), this mechanical test effectively reduces the
reporters' privilege to an exhaustion requirement under which every Privacy Act
plaintiff can always get access to confidential sources eventually, no matter how
trivial or tenuous the plaintiffs claims. It leaves no room to consider the reporter's
interest in keeping her source a secret.
That mechanical approach, which converts a crucial constitutional privilege
into a mere exhaustion requirement, conflicts with the tests adopted by multiple
other Circuits, which require broad balancing to apply the reporter's privilege and
which consider many factors the D.C. Circuit refused to consider, including the public
interest in preserving the ability of reporters and ultimately the public to obtain
information from confidential sources. The First Circuit, for example, holds that
applying the reporter's privilege requires courts to broadly 'balance the potential
harm to the free flow of information that might result [from disclosure] against the
asserted need for the requested information." Bruno, 633 F.2d at 595—96. That
includes 'the importance to the [journalist's] continued newsgathering effectiveness
of preserving the source's confidentiality." ld. at 597—98. Ms. Herridge presented
evidence explaining that disclosing her source(s) would destroy her ability to function
16

as a national security investigative journalist, App. 82a—85a, but the courts below
refused to consider that information.
The D.C. Circuit's approach departs from the First Circuit's in other ways.
While the D.C. Circuit considered whether Plaintiffs Privacy Act claims were
"frivolous," id. 60a—61a, it forbade any further examination into the merits of those
claims, id. 61a—62a. The First Circuit, however, expressly holds that a 'finding that
plaintiffs claim is not frivolous" "does not terminate the sensitive balancing process."
Bruno, 633 F.2d at 599 n.17. Instead, the First Circuit requires that, before
overcoming the privilege, "plaintiff should show that it can establish jury issues on
the essential elements of its case not the subject of the contested discovery." ld. at
597. In other words, the plaintiffs claims should be tested on partial summary
judgment to determine whether they will entirely (or mostly) collapse. See id.
(elements of plaintiffs claim should be "established as a jury issue before discovery
is compelled"). Ms. Herridge argued for precisely such testing of Plaintiffs case on
partial summary judgment, but the D.C. Circuit refused to consider it.
The First Circuit has also acknowledged that "there may be cases where
revelation of sources will threaten physical or other harm that will be quite
disproportionate to a plaintiffs litigation needs." Bruno, 633 F.2d at 595. The D.C.
Circuit, however, forbade considering such factors. Ms. Herridge submitted
declarations detailing the significant risk that Plaintiff was engaged in espionage for
China and the risks involved in forcing disclosure to her of the identity of
(presumptively) government personnel with knowledge of counterespionage
17

investigations. App. 93a—104a. The D.C. Circuit refused even to consider such
national security harms from the disclosure of confidential sources in this case.
The First Circuit is not alone in requiring a broader balancing of interests. The
Fourth Circuit applies a full-fledged balancing test. It has set out three factors to be
considered—relevance, exhaustion, and whether the plaintiff has a "compelling
interest in the information"—but has cautioned that those factors do not end the
inquiry. Ashcraft v. Conoco, Inc., 218 F.3d 282, 287—88 & n. 12 (4th Cir. 2000). Even
where a plaintiff shows a compelling interest, the "compelling nature of the interest
[in disclosure] would have to be balanced against the reporter's interest in protecting
the confidentiality of his sources." ld. at 288 n. 12.
The Ninth Circuit broadly requires that the "First Amendment privilege and
the opposing need for disclosure be judicially weighed in light of the surrounding
facts, and a balance struck to determine where lies the paramount interest," Shoen
v. Shoen, 5 F.3d 1289, 1293 (9th Cir. 1993) (quotation omitted), and the Tenth Circuit
has similarly endorsed a 'balancing test," while identifying four non-exhaustive
factors "[a]mong the factors that the trial court must consider," Grandbouche v.
Clancy, 825 F.2d 1463, 1466-67 (10th Cir. 1987).
State courts of last resort have also held that the First Amendment reporter's
privilege requires a broad balancing of interests.6 The Supreme Judicial Court of
Maine has expressly adopted the First Circuit's approach from Bruno. See, e.g., In re
6 There are relatively few state supreme court decisions addressing the contours of the First
Amendment reporte/s privilege because most States have adopted robust reporteFs privilege
protections by statute. See infra nn. 11, 12.
18

Letellier, 578 A.2d 722, 726 (Me. 1990). The Louisiana Supreme Court has explained
that, even in the criminal context, after the government has shown that a reporter's
information is "necessary" for a case, the court still must "balance" that need against
"the possible 'chilling effect' the disclosure will have on the freedom of the press and
the ability to gather news" and that "additional weight should be given to the
reporter's interest when the information concerns his investigation of or criticism of
the government." In re Grand Jury Proc. (Ridenhour), 520 So. 2d 372, 376 (La. 1988).
The split in authority is further deepened by the Seventh Circuit, which holds
that there is no First Amendment reporter's privilege. McKevitt v. Pallasch, 339 F.3d
530, 532-33 (7th Cir. 2003); see Cruz v. Guevara, 801 F. supp. 3d 767, 774 (N.D. 111.
2024) ("[NIO federal reporter's privilege exists in the Seventh Circuit.").
These divergent approaches to a constitutionally based privilege present an
important question of constitutional law that should be resolved by this Court. The
Court last addressed the First Amendment reporter's privilege in Branzburg v.
Hayes, in which a divided Court held that a reporter did not have an absolute First
Amendment privilege to refuse to appear before a federal grand jury pursuant to a
subpoena. 408 U.S. 665, 709 (1972). Justice Powell, who provided the fifth vote for
the majority, wrote separately to explain that, while there was no First Amendment
right to refuse to appear, reporters are not "without constitutional rights with respect
to the ...
safeguarding of their sources." ld. at 709—10 (Powell, J., concurring). He
explained that, when those rights are implicated, "the asserted claim to privilege
should be judged on its facts by the striking of a proper balance between freedom of
19

the press and the obligation of all citizens to give relevant testimony with respect to
criminal conduct" and that the balance would have to be struck on a "case-by-case
basis." ld. at 709—10 & n. * (Powell, J. , concurring); see Marks v. United States, 430
U.S. 188, 193 (1977).7
The Court has never addressed the reporter's privilege in a civil case,8 and as
explained above, in the absence of further guidance since Justice Powell's lone
concurrence over fifty years ago, the courts of appeals and state courts have adopted
widely divergent approaches to the privilege. There is no reason that the protection
afforded by the First Amendment should vary so drastically based upon the
geographic circuit in which reporter finds himself. Instead, there is a reasonable
probability that four Justices will agree that guidance from this Court is badly needed
to establish a uniform standard for applying this important constitutional protection
that is vital for preserving the functioning of the press.
B. The Decision Below Deepens a Circuit Split over Whether a Non-
Constitutional Reporter's Privilege Exists under the Authority
Conveyed by Federal Rule of Evidence 501.
There is likewise a reasonable probability that this Court will grant certiorari
to resolve the question whether, under the auspices of Federal Rule of Evidence 501,
reporters possess a non-constitutional evidentiary privilege against compelled
disclosure of confidential sources and information. This question has divided the

dissenting).

20

Courts of Appeals. Compare Riley v. City of Chester, 612 F.2d 708, 714—15 (3d Cir.
1979) (recognizing a privilege under common-law principles), with United States v.
Sterling, 724 F.3d 482, 505 (4th Cir. 2013) (rejecting such a privilege); United States
v. LaRouche Campaign, 841 F.2d 1176, 1178 n.4 (1st Cir. 1988) (same); Price v. Time,
Inc., 416 F.3d 1327, 1342 (11th Cir. 2005) ("[T]he common law is that there is no
confidential source privilege.").9
Like the D.C. Circuit, several courts of appeals have squarely held that "there
is no ... common-law privilege that protects [a journalist] from having to respond to
the government's subpoena and give what evidence he has." Sterling, 724 F.3d at
505. The Third Circuit, by contrast, has held that "journalists have a federal common
law privilege, albeit qualified, to refuse to divulge their sources." Riley, 612 F.2d at
715. That common-law privilege derived from "[t]he strong public policy which
supports the unfettered communication to the public of information," embodied in the
First Amendment, and the views of the states on the question of reporters'
evidentiary privileges. ld. Even still, the Third Circuit explained that "there are
countervailing interests which will suffice to transcend the journalist's privilege." ld.
Drawing on Justice Powell's Branzburg concurrence, the Third Circuit held that to
overcome the privilege, a litigant must show "a demonstrated, specific need for
evidence." ld. at 716 (quotation omitted). Then, the court must "balance on one hand
the policies which give rise to the privilege and their applicability to the facts at hand

First Amendment or federal common law. Gonzales v. NBC, Inc., 194 F.3d 29, 35 n.6 (2d Cir. 1999).
21

against the need for the evidence sought to be obtained." ld.
That disagreement is not academic. In this case, the D.C. Circuit flatly rejected
a common-law reporter's privilege. App. 63a—64a. By contrast, had this case arisen
in the Third Circuit, Herridge would likely have been privileged from being forced to
disclose her source(s). Any arguable need for this information would be outweighed
by the societal interests justifying the privilege (which the D.C. Circuit refused to
consider). Authorizing compelled disclosure of confidential sources in the national-
security context would seriously undermine the freedom of the press. While all
reporting relies on the ability to use and protect confidential sources, Riley, 612 F.2d
at 714; Baker v. F & F Inv., 470 F.2d 778, 782 (2d Cir. 1972), that dynamic is
especially pronounced in the national-security context. National security reporters,
like Herridge, inherently must rely on confidential sources. The pervasiveness of
classification and confidentiality in the national security realm means that few—if
any—sources will be willing to provide information to journalists without meaningful
guarantees that their identities will be protected. If reporters can be forced to disclose
their sources, few in the government will be willing to provide important information
to the press on matters of great public significance. That problem is particularly
acute when the compulsion to disclose can occur even in low-stakes civil suits brought
by private parties. Permitting such disclosure harms not only journalists, but also
the public at large, through loss of critical information about their government's
affairs. See N.Y. Times Co., 403 U.S. at 717 (Black, J. , concurring).
Under Riley, the balance is not even close: While Plaintiffs interest in
22

compelling Herridge to testify is minimal, the costs of compelling her testimony
would be substantial. In service of advancing a civil suit that may yet collapse on
other grounds or lead to recovering only paltry sums of money, the D.C. Circuit's rule
risks undermining critical newsgathering methods and hamstringing the free press
in its service to our democracy. A court applying Riley would likely find that the
privilege had not been overcome and would not have compelled Herridge to testify.
The stark disagreement on the existence of a federal common-law evidentiary
privilege for reporters under Federal Rule of Evidence 501 can only be resolved by
this Court. There is a reasonable probability that the Court will agree to review the
D.C. Circuit's decision to resolve that conflict. Sup. Ct. R. IO.
II. There Is at Least a Fair Prospect that the Court Would Reverse.
A. There Is a Fair Prospect the Court Would Reject the D.C.
Circuit's Mechanical Test for the First Amendment Reporter's
Privilege.
There is also at least a "fair prospect," Hollingsworth, 558 U.S. at 190, that this
Court would reverse the D.C. Circuit and hold that the First Amendment reporters'
privilege is not a mere exhaustion requirement under which every plaintiff who needs
the information can always get access to a reporter's confidential sources eventually,
no matter how tenuous or trivial the plaintiffs underlying claim. As explained below,
when journalists' confidential sources are disclosed in litigation, there are significant
societal costs in terms of injury to the functioning of the press and the public's ability
to receive information. That is why most circuits that have addressed the issue
recognize that courts should balance the litigant's need against the harm to First
23

Amendment values that follows from compelled disclosure. This Court is more likely
to adopt that approach, which calls for both a genuine balancing of interests and for
testing elements of the plaintiffs case on summary judgment before disclosure of
confidential sources is compelled.
This Court has acknowledged that reporters are "entitled to some
constitutional protection of the confidentiality of [their] sources." Pell v. Procunier,
417 U.S. 817, 834 (1974). It could hardly be otherwise given the First Amendment's
distinct protection for "the press." And as many lower courts have recognized, the
First Amendment reporter's privilege reflects that textual commitment and is critical
because there are significant costs to society when reporters are forced to disclose
confidential sources. "If reporters were routinely required to divulge the identities of
their sources, the free flow of newsworthy information would be restrained and the
public's understanding of important issues and events would be hampered in ways
inconsistent with a healthy republic." Ashcraft, 218 F.3d at 287; see also, e.g., Miller
v. Transamerican Press, Inc., 621 F.2d 721, 725 (5th Cir. 1980), opinion supplemented
on denial of reh'g, 628 F.2d 932 (5th Cir. 1980) ("[F]orced disclosure of journalists'
sources might deter informants from giving their stories to newsmen ... "
Simply
put, journalists rely on confidential sources for information, especially information
about the government. When journalists are compelled to disclose their sources in
litigation, it has a chilling effect that dries up the flow of information to the press and
prevents the press from fulfilling its "essential role in our democracy ' of "bar[ing] the
secrets of government and inform[ing] the people." N.Y. Times Co., 403 U.S. at 717
24

(Black, J., concurring). In no context is that more critical than in the national-
security context, where reporting depends on the ability to maintain confidences.
Given these substantial costs, the majority of circuits to address the matter
recognize that a litigant's claimed need for disclosing a source should be balanced
against the harm that will follow for the functioning of the press. In the decision
below, by contrast, the D.C. Circuit rejected any balancing of interests in favor of a
mechanical test that turns solely on whether the information is "central" to the
plaintiffs case (i.e., whether the plaintiff actually needs the information to make his
case) and whether the plaintiff has exhausted alternative avenues for getting the
information. That approach effectively reduces the test to an exhaustion requirement
under which every plaintiff who needs access to a source always gets access
eventually, no matter how trivial the plaintiffs underlying claim. There is least a
fair prospect that five members of this Court would agree that approach is
insufficiently protective of the First Amendment values at stake. Two aspects of the
test applied by other circuits (and rejected by the D.C. Circuit) are likely to prevail.
First, the majority of circuits that have addressed the issue call for genuinely
balancing a litigant's asserted need for a reporter's confidential source against the
"potential harm to the free flow of information [to the press] that might result" from
forced disclosure. Bruno, 633 F.2d at 596. Such a balancing necessarily
acknowledges that, in some scenarios, a litigant's claim may simply not involve a
substantial enough interest to justify incurring the societal costs involved in
overcoming the First Amendment reporter's privilege.
25

There is at least a fair prospect that this Court would adopt such a balancing
approach rather than the mechanical quasi-exhaustion test applied below. The D.C.
Circuit, for example, acknowledged that Plaintiffs claim may ultimately amount to
nothing more than a claim for $1,000 in statutory damages—yet held that Plaintiff
should still get access to Ms. Herridge's confidential source(s). App. 61a—62a. There
is at least a fair prospect that this Court would not agree that a claim for a nominal
$1,000 in damages warrants incurring the harms to the press that follow from
compelling disclosure of confidential sources.
The D.C. Circuit's absolutist approach is especially wrongheaded when one
also considers the impact that compelling disclosure of source(s) would have on Ms.
Herridge's ability to function as a national security reporter. As the First Circuit has
explained, a court should consider specifically "the importance to the [journalist's]
continued newsgathering effectiveness of preserving the source's confidentiality."
Bruno, 633 F.2d at 597—98. Here, Ms. Herridge introduced uncontested evidence that
her career as a national security reporter would be destroyed if she is compelled to
hand over her national security source(s) to a former colonel in the PLA. App. 82a—
85a. No national security sources would ever trust Ms. Herridge (or other national
security reporters) again if she does that. The D.C. Circuit refused even to consider
the cost to Ms. Herridge of compelling disclosure to Plaintiff, let alone the broader
negative impacts on newsgathering in the national security space. There is at least
a fair prospect, however, that five members of this Court would agree that these are
relevant factors to weigh in the balance.
26

This case also presents unique dangers related to compelled disclosure of

B. There Is a Fair Prospect that the Court Would Recognize a Non-
Constitutional Privilege Under FRE 501.
If this Court granted certiorari, there is also a fair prospect that it would
reverse the D.C. Circuit's decision and recognize the existence of a non-constitutional
evidentiary privilege for reporters under FRE 501 against the compelled disclosure
of their sources. That recognition, expressly authorized by Congress in Rule 501,
would align federal law with the law of 48 states and the District of Columbia.
In determining whether to recognize a common-law evidentiary privilege
under Rule 501, this Court considers two main factors. First, it assesses whether the
proposed privilege advances a "public good transcending the normally predominant
principle of utilizing all rational means for ascertaining truth." Jaffee, 518 U.S. at 9
(quoting Trammel v. United States, 445 U.S. 40, 50 (1980)). Second, it looks to the
"policy decisions of the States" with respect to state-level evidentiary privileges. ld.
at 12. "[T]he existence of a consensus among the States indicates that 'reason and
experience' support recognition of the privilege." ld. at 13 (quoting Fed. R. Evid. 501).
Thus, in Jaffee, this Court placed heavy weight on the fact that "all 50 States and the
District of Columbia ha[d] enacted into law some form of psychotherapist privilege."
ld. at 12.
The reporter's privilege advances critical societal interests. "An untrammeled
press [is] a vital source of public information, and an informed public is the essence
of working democracy." Minneapolis Star & Tribune Co. v. Minn. Comm'r of Revenue,
460 U.S. 575, 585 (1983). "Historically, we have viewed freedom of speech and of the
press as indispensable to a free society and its government." Smith v. Daily Mail
31

Pub. Co., 443 U.S. 97, 106 (1979) (Rehnquist, J., concurring in the judgment).
"Compelled disclosure of confidential sources unquestionably threatens a journalist's
ability to secure information that is made available to him only on a confidential
basis." Baker v. F & F Inv., 470 F.2d 778, 782 (2d Cir. 1972). Without confidential
sources, reporters "could reprint government statements, but not ferret out
underlying disagreements among officials; they could cover public governmental
actions, but would have great difficulty getting potential whistleblowers to talk about
government misdeeds." In re Grand Subpoena, Judith Miller, 438 F.3d 1141, 1168
(D.C. Cir. 2006) (Tatel, J., concurring in the judgment). In short, "the deterrent effect
[of] such disclosure ... threatens [the] freedom of the press and the public's need to be
informed." Baker, 470 F.2d at 782. "It thereby undermines values which traditionally
have been protected by federal courts applying federal public policy." ld.
These interests are equal or greater in importance to the interests involved in
the psychotherapist-patient privilege this Court recognized in Jaffee. Jaffee
recognized a need for a psychotherapist-patient privilege because the work of a
psychotherapist involves an "imperative need for confidence and trust." 518 U.S. at
10. "Effective psychotherapy ... depends upon an atmosphere of confidence and trust
in which the patient is willing to make a frank and complete disclosure of facts,
emotions, memories, and fears." ld. In that context, "the mere possibility of
disclosure may impede development of the confidential relationship necessary for
successful treatment." ld. Just so here. Cultivation of relationships between a
journalist and confidential sources likewise depends on an "atmosphere of confidence
32

and trust." ld. Confidentiality is often "essential" for sources to be willing to provide
information to journalists, Zerilli v. Smith, 656 F.2d 705, 711 (D.C. Cir. 1981); sources
will not be willing to provide information of vital public importance to journalists if
they must fear that the journalist will be subject to compulsory process and their
names will be identified in open court. Baker, 470 F.3d at 782. Indeed, "the mere
possibility of disclosure" will have a significant "deterrence effect" which "threatens
[the] freedom of the press and the public's need to be informed." Jaffee, 518 U.S. at
10; Baker, 470 F.3d at 782.
"[T]he existence of a consensus among the States indicates that 'reason and
experience' support recognition of the privilege." Jaffee, 518 U.S. at 13; Fed. R. Evid.
501 (making "reason and experience" the benchmark for recognition of evidentiary

compelled disclosure of their sources. 23 jurisdictions recognize an absolute privilege
against compelled disclosure of a reporter's sources in civil cases.ll 26 more recognize

near-uniform consensus among states concerning the need for a reporte€s privilege shows that the
state of the common law is no longer what it was in 1972.
34

order. Jaffee, 518 U.S. at 9. It serves important "public ends." ld. at 11. And it is
supported by a nationwide consensus among states that such a privilege is necessary
to protect legitimate newsgathering operations. ld. at 13.
III. Ms. Herridge Will Suffer Irreparable Harm Absent a Stay.
Absent a stay, Ms. Herridge will suffer irreparable harm because the Contempt
Order requires her to disclose her confidential source(s) in violation of her First
Amendment rights. Circuit Justices considering similar stay requests concerning
forced disclosure of confidential sources have had little difficulty finding that the
threat of disclosure constituted irreparable harm warranting a stay. In re Roche, 448
U.S. 1312, 1316 (1980) (Brennan, J., in chambers).
It is well settled that "[t]he loss of First Amendment freedoms, for even
minimal periods of time, unquestionably constitutes irreparable injury." Roman
Catholic Diocese of Brooklyn v. Cuomo, 592 U.S. 14, 19 (2020) (quoting Elrod v. Burns,
427 U.S. 347, 373 (1976) (plurality)). And this Court has routinely "shown a special
solicitude for applicants who seek stays of actions threatening a significant
impairment of First Amendment interests." N.Y. Times Co. v. Jascalevich, 439 U.S.
1331, 1333 (1978) (Marshall, J., in chambers).
If the order below were carried into effect, Ms. Herridge's First Amendment
rights would be violated, her promise(s) of confidentiality would be irretrievably
breached, the identity of her source(s) would be irrevocably disclosed, and no court
could ever make the identity of the source(s) secret again. The "cat [will be] out of
the bag." In re Kellogg Brown & Root, Inc., 756 F.3d 754, 761 (D.C. Cir. 2014)
35

(Kavanaugh, J.). Ms. Herridge would lose "confidentiality ... for all time," and "[t]he
status quo could never be restored." Providence Journal Co. v. FBI, 595 F.2d 889,
890 (1st Cir. 1979). Not surprisingly, courts have recognized that the disclosure of
confidential information is, by its nature, irreparable because "once ... putatively
protected material is disclosed, the very right sought to be protected has been
destroyed." In re Sealed Case No. 98-3077, 151 F.3d 1059, 1065 (D.C. Cir. 1998).
In addition, damage to Ms. Herridge's reputation as a reporter who keeps her
promises of confidentiality would be permanent and beyond repair, thus crippling her
ability to carry on her work as an Emmy-winning investigative reporter in the
national security field. See App. 85a.
Plaintiff argued below that Ms. Herridge does not face any irreparable harm
because she has an option to avoid immediate disclosure: defying the Contempt Order
and incurring fines of $800 a day. But that is no answer. Every party subject to a
court order technically has the "option" of disobeying and incurring contempt
sanctions. That choice is never treated as eliminating irreparable harm that would
flow from implementing the order. See, e.g., United States v. Philip Morris Inc., 314
F.3d 612, 622 (D.C. Cir. 2003) (assuming compliance with disclosure order to find
irreparable harm), abrogated on other grounds by Mohawk Indus., Inc. v. Carpenter,
558 U.S. 100 (2009). Indeed, Circuit Justices have expressly rejected the idea that a
reporte€s "option" of incurring contempt sanctions can eliminate the irreparable
harm that comes from an order requiring disclosure of confidential sources. In re
Roche, 448 U.S. at 1316 (Brennan, J., in chambers). The question on a stay is always
36

whether the order below, if carried into effect, would cause irreparable harm pending
appeal if the order is later overturned.
In addition, if there is no stay and Ms. Herridge is forced to disclose her
source(s), that would likely render this case moot. Once the source(s) are disclosed,
this Court could no longer provide Ms. Herridge any relief. The loss of the ability to
seek further review would itself compound the irreparable harm she faces. See, e.g.,
John Doe Agency v. John Doe Corp., 488 U.S. 1306, 1309 (1989) (Marshall, J., in
chambers) ("The fact that disclosure would moot .
. part of the Court of Appeals'
decision .
. would also create an irreparable injury?' justifying stay).
IV. The Balance of Equities and the Public Interest Favor a Stay.
Both the balance of equities and public interest strongly favor a stay. Cf.
Rostker v. Goldberg, 448 U.S. 1306, 1308 (1980) (Brennan, J., in chambers)
(considering these factors).
A stay will not harm Plaintiff, because it only "postpones the moment of
disclosure[,] assuming [plaintiff] prevails[,] by whatever period of time may be
required [l to hear and decide the appeal[.]" Providence Journal, 595 F.2d at 890. In
addition, Plaintiffs need for information is not time-sensitive. This case has been
pending for seven and a half years, and the district court's order has been stayed for
two and a half years. A short additional delay to allow this Court time to consider a
petition for certiorari will not harm Plaintiff. In particular, there is no impending
deadline after which the information from Ms. Herridge will no longer be useful.
The public interest also strongly favors a stay. Indeed, the broader public
37

interest in this case is underscored by the multiple amicus filings below. See, e.g.,
Amicus Brief of Sen. Ted Cruz, Chen v. FBI, No. 24-5050 (D.C. Cir. June 27, 2024);
Amicus Brief of The Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, Chen v. FBI, No.
24-5050 (D.C. Cir. July I, 2024). Plaintiff is seeking to uncover confidential source(s)
related to reporting on a counterintelligence probe. The First Amendment interest
in protecting the ability of investigative journalists to gather information from
confidential sources is at its zenith in such national security cases. In that context,
the need for confidentiality is especially acute because unauthorized leaks can carry
severe repercussions. As two-time Pulitzer Prize winning national security journalist
Steve Coll explained in a declaration below, the press "could not effectively report" on
matters of national security and international affairs without using confidential
sources. App. 87a 116. Based on his experience as a reporter focusing on national
security and international affairs, he explained that "it simply is not possible" to
contradict official government positions on these important topics—or to evaluate
leaks directed by high-level officials—without using confidential sources who have
access to protected information. ld. "16—8.
Given the secrecy surrounding national security matters, the public must
particularly rely on a vigorous free press to fulfill the "essential role in our democracy*'
of 'bar[ing] the secrets of government and inform[ing] the people." N. Y. Times Co.,
403 U.S. at 717 (Black, J., concurring). These interests will be irrevocably
compromised if Ms. Herridge is wrongly forced to reveal her source(s) before this
Court reviews the case, because that disclosure would have a broad chilling effect,
38

deterring potential sources and thereby hampering efforts of all investigative
journalists to report on the government. App. 88a 1[11. As courts have recognized,
"the press' function as a vital source of information is weakened whenever the ability
of journalists to gather news is impaired." Zerilli, 656 F.2d at 711. Such sources are
essential, moreover, for the press to inform the people about situations such as the
one in this case—where taxpayer dollars were funding a suspected former colonel in
the PLA while she collected information on U.S. servicemembers and made it
accessible from China.
The public interest also favors a stay because a remand could moot this case
by forcing Ms. Herridge to disclose her source(s). A stay is thus necessary to protect
this Court's jurisdiction and allow it to provide guidance on the appropriate test for
applying the First Amendment reporter's privilege. See, e.g., In re Roche, 448 U.S. at
1316 (Brennan, J., in chambers) (stay warranted in reporteßs privilege case because
disclosure of the source would "moot [applicant's] claim"); N.Y. Nat. Res. Def. Council,
Inc. v. Kleppe, 429 U.S. 1307, 1310 (1976) (Marshall, J., in chambers) ("Perhaps the
most compelling justification for a Circuit Justice to upset an interim decision by a
court of appeals [is] to protect this Court's power to entertain a petition for certiorari
before or after the final judgment of the Court of Appeals").
To the extent Plaintiffs Privacy Act suit may be viewed as also furthering some
public interest, cf. Contempt Order, App. 51a, a stay will not undermine that interest.
A stay will cause only a temporary delay while this Court addresses whether the
lower courts applied the correct test before ordering Ms. Herridge to disclose her
39

source(s). Whatever public interest inheres in the Privacy Act claim can be vindicated
after this Court's review—if the order below survives. Without a stay, by contrast,
the public interest in promoting the flow of information to the press by protecting
journalist's confidential sources would be irretrievably compromised if Ms. Herridge
is erroneously forced to disclose her source(s).
